definition: Protectionism is an economic and trade policy that favors domestic producers, workers, or industries by limiting foreign competition or giving domestic activity an advantage. Measures commonly described as protectionist include tariffs, quotas, import licenses, subsidies, local-content rules, government-procurement preferences, discriminatory taxes or regulations, and export restrictions. Protectionist policies may arise from nationalist, strategic, or social concerns, including the desire to safeguard critical industries, counter perceived unfair trade practices, or to prevent a global race to the bottom in labor and environmental standards. The label generally describes a policy's protective purpose, design, or economic effect; it does not itself identify the particular policy's legal authority. Supporters may defend protectionist measures as tools to preserve employment or critical capacity, respond to unfair trade, protect national security, reduce dependence on foreign suppliers, or give developing industries time to grow. Critics argue that such measures can raise prices, reduce choice, shelter inefficient firms, disrupt supply chains, invite retaliation, and shift costs to downstream businesses and consumers. The effects depend on the measure's design, duration, market conditions, and the responses of trading partners. In the United States, Article 1 of the Constitution gives Congress the power to impose duties and regulate commerce with foreign nations. Congress has enacted statutes delegating specified trade authorities to the executive branch. U.S. antidumping law authorizes duties when imported merchandise is sold at less than fair value and causes or threatens material injury to a U.S. industry. Countervailing-duty law addresses certain foreign-government subsidies. Section 201 safeguard law can authorize temporary relief when increased imports are a substantial cause of serious injury or threat of serious injury, even without a finding of unfair trade.
